meta.titre: Temperature measurement: thermometric properties and choosing an instrument

sections.contenu_markdown: A nurse at a health centre in Bamenda slides a small glass thermometer under a child's arm, waits a few minutes and reads 38.4 degrees. A farmer in Mbouda dips a different thermometer into a pot of palm oil to check it is hot enough for frying. Both people are measuring temperature, but they need different instruments. The GCE asks you to define temperature, to explain what makes a thermometer work, and to say why one design suits one job better than another, so this topic is worth easy marks.

items: Matter is made of particles that are always moving, and they move faster when the substance is hotter.
Most liquids and solids expand when they are heated.
Energy is measured in joules and the length of an object is measured in metres or millimetres.

sections.titre: Temperature, thermometric properties and the design of a thermometer
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Temperature** is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body. It tells us in which direction heat will flow: from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature. Its SI unit is the **kelvin (K)**; in everyday use we also use the degree Celsius ($^\circ\mathrm{C}$). **Heat** is different: it is a form of energy that flows because of a temperature difference, and it is measured in **joules (J)**.

**Thermometric property.** A thermometer works because some physical property changes steadily and measurably with temperature. Examples:

| Thermometer | Thermometric property |
|---|---|
| Liquid-in-glass (mercury or alcohol) | length of the liquid column |
| Resistance thermometer | electrical resistance of a metal wire |
| Thermocouple | e.m.f. produced at a junction |
| Constant-volume gas thermometer | pressure of the gas |

**The two fixed points.** To mark a scale we need two temperatures that are always the same: the **lower fixed point** (pure melting ice, $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and the **upper fixed point** (steam above boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure, $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). Steam is used for the upper point, not the boiling water itself, because dissolved impurities change the boiling temperature of the water but not the temperature of the steam above it.

**A good thermometric liquid** expands regularly, is easy to see (mercury is shiny, alcohol is dyed red), conducts heat well so it responds quickly, does not stick to the glass and stays liquid over a wide range.

**Sensitivity** is the movement of the thread per degree. It is increased by a *narrower bore* and a *larger bulb*; thin glass walls make the thermometer respond faster. The **range** is the interval between the lowest and highest temperatures it can measure.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must choose the liquid for a given job.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Mercury freezes at $-39\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and boils at $357\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so it suits high temperatures but not very cold ones. Alcohol freezes at $-115\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and boils at $78\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so it suits very low temperatures but not boiling water. Mercury is a better conductor and does not wet the glass; alcohol must be dyed to be seen.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how a clinical thermometer differs from a laboratory thermometer.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A clinical thermometer has (1) a **narrow range**, about $35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $42\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, which makes each degree occupy a long stretch of the stem; (2) a **constriction** (kink) near the bulb that stops the mercury from flowing back, so the reading stays after it is taken out of the mouth; (3) a thick, magnifying stem for easy reading. It must be **shaken** to push the mercury back before the next use. It is never placed in boiling water.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A school laboratory has two liquid-in-glass thermometers, A and B, with the same range. When the temperature of water rises by $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the thread of A moves $18\ \mathrm{mm}$ and the thread of B moves $27\ \mathrm{mm}$.

(a) Find the sensitivity of each thermometer in $\mathrm{mm}$ per $^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and say which is more sensitive.

(b) A technician must measure the temperature inside a freezer at about $-60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Choose between a mercury thermometer and an alcohol thermometer and give a reason.

etapes.justification: Sensitivity is the distance moved by the thread for each degree of temperature change.
Divide the movement by the temperature change with units.
Same method for the second thermometer.
The larger the movement per degree, the easier it is to read small changes.
etapes.resultat_markdown: B moves $1.5$ times as far per degree, so B is more sensitive (it probably has a narrower bore).

etapes.justification: Mercury freezes at $-39\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, which is above $-60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, while alcohol stays liquid down to $-115\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The mercury would be solid in the freezer; alcohol would still be liquid.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a)** A: $0.60\ \mathrm{mm}/^\circ\mathrm{C}$; B: $0.90\ \mathrm{mm}/^\circ\mathrm{C}$; B is more sensitive. **(b)** Use the **alcohol** thermometer because mercury freezes at $-39\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

items.erreur_markdown: “Temperature is the amount of heat in a body, measured in joules.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Heat is energy (joules) that flows because of a temperature difference. Temperature is the degree of hotness, not the quantity of energy.
items.correction_markdown: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body; its SI unit is the kelvin. Heat is a form of energy measured in joules.

items.erreur_markdown: “The upper fixed point is the temperature of the boiling water itself.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Impurities dissolved in water raise its boiling temperature, so the result would not always be the same. The steam above it stays at the same temperature.
items.correction_markdown: The upper fixed point is the temperature of **steam** above boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure, $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

items.erreur_markdown: “A mercury thermometer can be used to measure $-60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Mercury freezes at $-39\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so at $-60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the thread is solid and cannot move.
items.correction_markdown: Use alcohol (freezing point $-115\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) for very low temperatures.

items.erreur_markdown: “To make a thermometer more sensitive, use a wider bore.”
items.pourquoi_faux: A wide bore needs much more liquid to fill it, so the thread moves only a short distance for each degree. The change is smaller, not bigger.
items.correction_markdown: Use a **narrower** bore and a **larger** bulb so that the same expansion gives a longer movement of the thread.

items.erreur_markdown: “The SI unit of temperature is the degree Celsius.”
items.pourquoi_faux: The Celsius degree is a very common unit but the SI base unit of temperature is the kelvin.
items.correction_markdown: State: SI unit of temperature = kelvin (K); the degree Celsius ($^\circ\mathrm{C}$) is a convenient unit in everyday use.

items.enonce_markdown:
Name the thermometric property that is used in each of these thermometers.

(a) a mercury-in-glass thermometer

(b) a thermocouple thermometer

(c) a constant-volume gas thermometer
items.solution_markdown:
A thermometric property is a property that changes steadily with temperature.

(a) Mercury-in-glass: the **length of the mercury column**.

(b) Thermocouple: the **e.m.f. (voltage) produced** at the junction.

(c) Constant-volume gas thermometer: the **pressure of the gas**.

items.enonce_markdown:
The thread of a liquid-in-glass thermometer moves $4.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ when the temperature changes by $15\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

(a) Calculate its sensitivity in $\mathrm{mm}/^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

(b) By how many millimetres will the thread move when the temperature changes by $40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?

A clinical thermometer has a stem scale from $35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $42\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ occupying $7.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. A laboratory thermometer has a scale from $-10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ occupying $24\ \mathrm{cm}$. Both are uniform.

(a) Calculate the sensitivity of each in $\mathrm{cm}/^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and compare them.

(b) How far from the $35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ mark is the thread of the clinical thermometer when a patient has a temperature of $38.4\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?

(c) Give two other features of the clinical thermometer that the laboratory thermometer lacks.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Clinical: range $=42-35=7\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so sensitivity $=7.0/7=$ **$1.0\ \mathrm{cm}/^\circ\mathrm{C}$**.
Laboratory: range $=110-(-10)=120\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so sensitivity $=24/120=$ **$0.20\ \mathrm{cm}/^\circ\mathrm{C}$**.
The clinical thermometer is $1.0/0.20=$ **5 times more sensitive**.

(b) Distance $=(38.4-35)\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\times 1.0\ \mathrm{cm}/^\circ\mathrm{C}=$ **$3.4\ \mathrm{cm}$**.

(c) It has a **constriction** near the bulb which keeps the mercury in place after the reading, so it must be shaken down before reuse; it also has a **narrow range** close to body temperature (and a magnifying stem for easy reading).

items_markdown: Temperature is the degree of hotness of a body (SI unit: kelvin); heat is energy measured in joules.
A thermometer uses a thermometric property (column length, resistance, e.m.f., gas pressure) that changes steadily with temperature.
Fixed points: melting ice ($0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and steam at standard pressure ($100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$); steam is used because impurities do not change its temperature.
Sensitivity = thread movement per degree; it is increased by a narrow bore and a large bulb. Mercury suits high temperatures, alcohol suits very low ones.
A clinical thermometer has a narrow range ($35$ to $42\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and a constriction that holds the reading.
